                                          PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                              §               BEFORE THE
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                           §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                         §                OF TEXAS

                   ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY’S COMMENTS
              ON COMMISSION STAFF’S RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT

          Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) files this response to the Rule 25.194

discussion draft issued by the staff (“Staff”) of the Public Utility Commission of Texas

(“Commission”) in this project on December 1, 2025. Oncor includes in these comments: (1) a

redline version of the discussion draft (Attachment B) and (2) a diagram showing the discussion

draft load interconnection process and Oncor’s recommended changes (Attachment C). Oncor

appreciates the opportunity to assist with Staff’s efforts to adopt new rules that implement Senate

Bill 6.

                 I.    COMMENTS ON RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT

1. Section (h)(9): interconnecting customers should not be responsible for system upgrades
   because it stifles growth, introduces unnecessary complexity, and does not allocate costs
   based on current or future benefit.1
          Section (h)(9)’s imposition of system upgrade costs on interconnecting large load

customers would be a drastic change in the way the Commission assigns transmission project costs.

The Texas “connect-and-manage” system has contributed to the rapid growth of the Texas grid by

democratizing the costs of expansion and keeping the barriers to entry low for new generators and

loads. This ease of access has spurred economic development. Transitioning to a system where

an incremental interconnecting large load customer must pay for resultant system upgrades



          1
         Note, Oncor recently responded to a question related to this issue posed by the Commission Staff in
Docket No. 58484. See Evaluation of Transmission Cost Recovery, Docket No. 58484, Oncor Electric Delivery’s
Response to Commission Staff’s Second Set of Questions for Comments (Nov. 25, 2025) at 3-5.



ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT - Page 1 of 14
                                                                                                               1
 introduces a first-mover problem that could stifle economic growth and slow grid expansion, both

in direct opposition to the goals of Senate Bill 6.

        Oncor recommends eliminating the language from the rule that requires large load

customers to pay contribution in aid of construction (“CIAC”) for system upgrades that “would

not be required but for the interconnecting large load customer.” Networked assets, including

those constructed as part of system upgrades, inherently benefit the entirety of the Texas grid, not

just the incremental customer whose interconnection happens to trigger the need for a system

upgrade. Oncor agrees that interconnecting customers should be required to pay CIAC equal to

the costs of direct interconnection facilities, the facilities that will only be used by the

interconnecting load. Any costs related to transmission facilities that are used or could be used in

the future by other customers should be system costs because of their wider benefit.

        Oncor recommends that the Commission require CIAC for the tap, bay, and/or breaker that

directly serves the new load. Regardless of growth on the system or the integration of other loads

in the vicinity, these limited facilities will only serve this individual load and thus are properly the

responsibility of that load through a CIAC payment. Radial lines and wider system upgrades on

the other hand, could be used to serve and benefit other customers in the future. For example,

assume a new load requires a ten mile radial line to a tap point to establish new service. The tap

itself would be the interconnection cost because it would only be used by this one load. The ten

mile radial transmission line would be a system cost because it could be used by other customers

in the future. The first customer for which the transmission line is extended does not own that

line; the line is available for public service. It is a piece of the ERCOT grid that can be utilized to

serve any customer at any time. When another customer wishes to tap or take service from that




ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT - Page 2 of 14
                                                                                                       2
 line, the utility will provide such service. This is why it is inequitable for the first load customer

to be required to provide CIAC for the ten mile radial line.

        Over the last twenty years, Oncor’s west Texas transmission system has grown piece by

piece, one radial customer service extension after another. Through this exact process, Oncor has

extended transmission level service to countless new customers in the Permian and Delaware

basins. For example, Oncor extended 138 kilovolt (“kV”) transmission service from Wink to

Culberson to meet customer needs. At first, this facility was a new, radial, single-circuit

transmission line. See Culberson Loop 2012 (Attachment A). A few years later, this radial

transmission line was rebuilt to a 138 kV double-circuit line to serve the needs of various new

customers. A line was then built to Barstow as the first leg of the loop back to Culberson for

customer needs. See Culberson Loop 2016 (Attachment A). The line was eventually looped from

Wink to Culberson and back into Yucca Drive, creating a new dually fed 138 kV transmission loop,

known as the Culberson Loop, through a previously unserved area of Texas. See Culberson Loop

2018 (Attachment A). Two additional loops were then built off the Culberson Loop in the same

manner to meet customer needs. These loops extended service to Owl Hills and Kyle Ranch,

allowing hundreds of MWs of customers to be served. See Culberson Loop 2022 (Attachment A).

While each extension of the 138 kV service was originally undertaken to serve a single new

customer, other customers eventually developed and were served by the same transmission line

and stations. Further, Oncor stepped down the voltage to distribution levels and also served

distribution load from these new transmission fed stations. This is why interconnecting customers

should be required to pay CIAC based on who could use the facility—not just who is using the

facility initially.




ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT - Page 3 of 14
                                                                                                     3
        Further, the language of Section (h)(9) related to CIAC for system upgrades should be

removed because it introduces unnecessary accounting and modeling complexities. Oncor is not

aware of any method for attributing a share of CIAC paid by a prior interconnecting customer to a

currently interconnecting customer under Section (h)(9)(C). And any method promises to

introduce a high level of complexity and burden on utilities. Similarly, deciding which system

upgrades “would not be required but for the interconnecting large load customer” introduces

significant modeling challenges that will likely cause delays for interconnecting large loads –

before beginning construction on the facilities required to directly interconnect the large load, the

interconnecting utility would be required to model which future system upgrades are “but-for”

upgrades and decide how much these upgrades will cost.

       Moreover, large loads often change hands before completing their load ramps and after.

The draft rule would require utilities to facilitate CIAC payments from a new interconnecting

customer back to the customer that initially paid CIAC for an interconnected load that may have

changed hands two or three times during the ensuing years. Utilities should dedicate their

resources to providing service, not to becoming a financial institution.

       Generally, CIAC should not represent a large burden on interconnecting large loads given

the rigor of the other financial commitment requirements (per MW security, security for significant

equipment or services, etc.). The barrier the discussion draft rule creates for large loads is simply

too high. If the Commission desires to increase the portion of costs paid by large loads, there are

more efficient and appropriate methods of reallocating costs than dramatically expanding the scope

of CIAC. For one, adjusting transmission rates higher for large loads is a better method. The

Commission is currently working on reexamining transmission cost allocation in Docket No.




ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT - Page 4 of 14
                                                                                                    4
 58484 – the new rule proposed in that docket is a far more appropriate means of allocating more

transmission costs to large loads than dramatically increasing CIAC requirements in this docket.

2. Section (c): the interconnecting customer should be required to execute a Large Load
   Interconnection Study agreement with the interconnecting utility prior to the utility
   beginning its study of the load.
       Currently, Oncor and other utilities require a Discretionary Services Agreement to be

executed prior to any study of an interconnecting large load. This agreement, among other things,

sets out the terms under which the interconnecting customer pays the initial study costs. Oncor

believes that a large load interconnection study agreement of this type should be a required first

step in the interconnection process set out by the discussion draft. Oncor believes an agreement is

necessary to memorialize the terms of study fee payment and the disclosures required under

Section (c).

3. Section (d)(2): if a large load that requests additional capacity or significantly adjusts
   its schedule after the start of the large load interconnection study, the interconnecting
   utility should have the discretion to restart the study.
       First, Oncor recommends that language be added to Section (d)(2) to require payment of

an additional study fee for schedule adjustments. Like changes in requested or contracted peak

demand, schedule adjustments can require re-study or additional studies.           Second, Oncor

recommends that language be added to Section (d)(2) that explicitly recognizes that

interconnecting utilities have the discretion to treat changes in requested or contracted peak

demand or schedule as requiring full re-study of the interconnecting load.

4. Sections (d), (e), and (f): interconnecting utilities should be permitted to require the
   intermediate agreement to be executed before or anytime during the utility study process.
       First, Oncor recommends that the agreement contemplated under Section (e) be renamed

the “Intermediate Agreement” because Oncor believes referring to that agreement as a

“discretionary services agreement” is somewhat misleading given the current usage of that term.



ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT - Page 5 of 14
                                                                                                   5
 As discussed, a discretionary services agreement is typically executed in advance of utility studies

and payment of the study fee.

       Second, Oncor recommends that the rule allow interconnecting utilities the discretion to

require the intermediate agreement be executed at any time during or prior to the utility’s study of

the interconnecting load. Today, Oncor requires security of $6.5 million, among other things, prior

to studying a large load in order to filter out speculative load modeling requests. Oncor sees the

intermediate agreement as having a similar function, albeit featuring potentially stronger filtering

mechanisms and protections. During times of high load interconnection demand, utilities should

have the discretion to filter loads before it studies them. In times of lower load interconnection

demand, this discretion would allow utilities to lower barriers to utility modeling by sliding back

the intermediate agreement requirement to later in the study process or immediately prior to

submitting the LLIS to ERCOT.

       Oncor also believes that the intermediate agreement requirement should be permitted to

slide backwards to allow for large loads that meet the numerous requirements of Section (e) to be

included in ERCOT’s load forecasts earlier. In Commission Staff’s discussion draft Rule 25.370

issued in Docket No. 58480, a large load will be included in ERCOT’s forecasts, if it executes an

intermediate agreement and meets various other requirements. Under Section (f) of the current

draft Rule 25.194, an interconnecting utility must submit the LLIS to ERCOT within 7 days of

executing the intermediate agreement. This means that a large load will only be included in

ERCOT’s models after it meets the numerous requirements under Section (e) and the

interconnecting utility completes all studies within an LLIS. This is much too late in the process

to begin including an interconnecting large load in the forecast. If a large load posts security,




ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT - Page 6 of 14
                                                                                                   6
 demonstrates site control, and makes the disclosures required in Section (e), it should be included

in ERCOT’s forecasts prior to the interconnecting utility conducting any studies.

       Finally, Oncor recommends that the language of Section (f) be changed to contemplate a

30-day deadline for an interconnecting utility to submit the large load interconnection study to

ERCOT after (i) the intermediate agreement has been executed and securitized and (ii) the utility

has completed its studies.     It often takes far more than 7 days to prepare the large load

interconnection study package for submission to ERCOT – utilities should be allotted sufficient

time to prepare these submissions.

5. Section (e)(2)(A): the heightened site control requirement of Section (e) should allow
   proof of site control via option to lease or executed lease for the duration of at least 5
   years after the expected time to reach peak demand.
       Oncor recommends that the ability to prove site control via an option to lease or a signed

and executed lease under Section (e)(2)(A)-(B) be increased to a longer minimum lease period

than 50% of the expected time to reach peak demand. Many load commissioning schedules

contemplate large loads reaching peak demand in under four years. In these cases, the currently

proposed requirement would allow developers to demonstrate site control with an option to lease

or a signed and executed lease of less than two years. This does not sufficiently demonstrate a

commitment to interconnection under a Section (e) agreement.              Oncor believes that this

requirement should be increased to require an interconnecting load to secure an option to lease or

sign and execute a lease of a duration lasting or at least 5 years after the load reaches peak demand.

6. Sections (e)(8)(B) and (h)(8): The requirements for the minimum forms of payment for
   financial security should be raised to ensure financial commitment.
       Oncor recommends that the Commission raise the requirements for the minimum forms of

payment for financial security in Sections (e)(8)(B) and (h)(8) of the discussion draft to ensure that

interconnecting customers are financially committed to interconnection. Specifically, Oncor



ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT - Page 7 of 14
                                                                                                     7
 recommends requiring a credit rating from Standard & Poor’s or Moody’s for a corporation or

parent corporation issuing a corporate or parental guaranty submitted by the interconnecting

customer as security. Oncor also recommends requiring a letter of credit from a major U.S.

commercial bank, or a U.S. branch office of a major foreign commercial bank, with a credit rating

of at least “A-” by Standard & Poor’s and “A3” by Moody’s Investor Service if the interconnecting

customer submits a letter of credit as security. Finally, Oncor recommends that language be added

to the rule to explicitly require an interconnecting customer to provide financial records or

statements requested by the interconnecting utility if the interconnecting customer submits a

corporate or parental guaranty as security.

7. Section (g)(4): The deadline for a customer to amend the large load interconnection
   study agreement and pay study costs after receiving notice of additional studies should
   be extended to 30 days after receiving a draft updated study agreement from the
   interconnecting utility.
       First, Oncor recommends that the language of Section (g)(4) be updated to reflect the

addition of the Large Load Interconnection Study Agreement, as proposed by Oncor in Section 2

of these comments. Second, the rule should be changed allow sufficient time for the parties to

amend the LLIS agreement and the customer to pay the additional fee once ERCOT identifies the

need for an additional study. A 10-day deadline does not leave enough time and is unnecessarily

burdensome on both the utility and customer. Oncor recommends a 30-day deadline instead.

8. Section (i)(1): The deadline for a utility to notify ERCOT after receiving a customer
   withdraw notice should be extended to 14 days.
       Oncor recommends that an interconnecting utility’s deadline for notifying ERCOT after an

interconnecting large load customer notifies the utility of its notice to withdraw is extended to 14

days. A 14-day deadline would lessen the administrative burden on interconnecting utilities

without negatively impacting the large load interconnection process. In general, the rule should




ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT - Page 8 of 14
                                                                                                   8
 allow interconnecting utilities to focus their efforts and resources on interconnecting new large

loads by not imposing short deadlines for removing large loads from the interconnection process.

9. Section (j): Capacity should be reallocated into the system-wide capacity bucket managed
   by ERCOT via batch studies.
          Oncor recommends that the Commission create a standardized capacity reallocation

process that not only dictates when a utility may reallocate capacity, but how and when the capacity

is reallocated. Oncor specifically supports recent efforts to centralize and standardize the capacity

reallocation process by moving capacity that can be reallocated into a system-wide bucket that is

managed by ERCOT. Oncor supports a reallocation process where ERCOT reallocates capacity

on a system-wide basis through a comprehensive batch study process, which can study load

interconnection requests in groups across the ERCOT system and identify where capacity is best

reallocated.

          If the Commission maintains the reallocation scheme found in the discussion draft, Oncor

recommends the incremental changes it proposes in Attachment B: (i) interconnecting utilities

have the option, and not the requirement, to reallocate the capacity of an interconnected large load

customer after the customer fails to meet a load commissioning plan milestone for 18 months and

(ii) interconnecting utilities are required to reallocate capacity after 48 months. This scheme

allows interconnecting utilities the flexibility to reallocate capacity when it has become clear that

an interconnected customer will not achieve its peak load but allows utilities to work with

customers who are experiencing delays in their load commissioning plans to hold capacity for up

to 48 months. The current rule is unnecessarily inflexible to reasonable load commissioning plan

delays.

10. Oncor recommends that the Commission prescribe a standard large load interconnection
    agreement.



ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT - Page 9 of 14
                                                                                                    9
        Executing an interconnection agreement is a key part of the large load interconnection

process that Senate Bill 6 requires the Commission to standardize. Currently, the terms of these

agreements vary widely.         These non-standardized interconnection agreements have created

uncertainty in the ERCOT process, as different utility agreements are treated disparately. Oncor

recommends that the Commission implement a standard large load interconnection agreement

similar in function to the existing standard generation interconnection agreement to solve this

problem. A standardized agreement will also promote equal access to the Texas grid by eliminating

the patchwork of current interconnection agreement terms.

                   II.    RESPONSES TO QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT

1. Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load customer
   is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how should the
   commission define those parameters?
       Yes, but the requirement should remain consistent with Senate Bill 6. Senate Bill 6 simply

requires a disclosure to the interconnecting utility if the request “would result in the customer

materially changing, delaying, or withdrawing the interconnection request.” 2 The Commission’s

rule should only require this finite disclosure. Also, ERCOT should be responsible, with any

necessary input from the interconnecting utility, for determining whether an interconnection

request is “substantially similar” under the parameters the Commission sets.

2. Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific
   information related to a substantially similar request for interconnection and allows a
   large load customer to anonymize competitively sensitive details. Should the commission
   list what is and is not competitively sensitive (e.g., load zone is not competitively sensitive
   information)? If so, what information should and should not be considered competitively
   sensitive such that the interconnecting utility and ERCOT can identify whether there is
   a duplicate request, or a request is unlikely to materialize?
       No comment.



       2
           PURA § 37.0561(d).


ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT - Page 10 of 14
                                                                                                10
 3. Should the commission require a large load customer to notify the interconnecting
   electric utility and ERCOT of any change to information that is initially disclosed in
   response to this rule or only material changes to the information disclosed? If only
   material changes, how should “material change” be defined?
       Oncor recommends that the Commission add a materiality qualifier to the language

requiring large load customers to report a change to information that is initially disclosed and

define what constitutes a material change. Without a materiality qualifier, compliance with this

subsection will be burdensome, especially with respect to changes in to large loads’ schedules for

phased energization of requested peak demand.         Loads commonly marginally modify their

schedules throughout the interconnection process. Small changes in peak load or timing should

not automatically require a disclosure. If the Commission requires frequent updates, this will result

in a substantial monitoring and reporting burden levied on both interconnecting customers and

utilities. Oncor recommends that the Commission set materiality qualifiers to require disclosure

if an interconnecting large load experiences (1) a 6-month change in load ramp or (2) a 75-MW

change in peak load.

4. Proposed subsection (k)(1) authorizes an interconnecting electric utility to refund 20%
   of a large load customer’s security after energization and ratably as the large load
   customer meets the milestones identified in the customer’s schedule for phased
   energization of its contracted load. Should the commission standardize the rate for
   refund for reaching milestones identified in the customer’s schedule for phased
   energization (e.g., 20% for each year of operations until the full amount of security is
   refunded)? If so, how should the commission standardize the refund?
       Yes. Oncor recommends that the Commission set a standard rate for refund related to

reaching milestones in the customer’s schedule for phased energization. However, Oncor does not

yet have an opinion on the specific methodology. Oncor looks forward to further discussion on

this point in the upcoming workshop.

5. Are changes to the commission’s other substantive rules necessary to align with this
   rulemaking? If so, what changes need to be made to which rules?




ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT - Page 11 of 14
                                                                                                   11
           Yes. 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(ii)(I) requires an amendment to be consistent with House Bill

5066 and Senate Bill 6. This rule contains a “quantifiable evidence” requirement that has been

overruled by statute now twice. First, in House Bill 5066 where the load to be considered by the

Commission was directly addressed and defined without a requirement for quantifiable evidence.

Now, in Senate Bill 6, the legislature has expressly provided precisely the requirements a load

must meet for consideration. This legacy rule language is both no longer consistent with Texas

law and no longer needed.

                                     III.    CONCLUSION

          Oncor appreciates the opportunity to assist with Staff’s evaluations pursuant to Senate

Bill 6.

1. Section (h)(9): interconnecting customers should not be responsible for system upgrades
   because it stilles growth, introduces unnecessary complexity, and does not allocate costs

          Section (h)(9)'s imposition of system upgrade costs on interconnecting large load

customers would be a drastic change in the way the Commission assigns transmission project costs.

The Texas "connect-and-manage" system has contributed to the rapid growth of the Texas grid by

democratizing the costs of expansion and keeping the barriers to entry low for new generators and

loads. This ease of access has spurred economic development. Transitioning to a system where

an incremental interconnecting large load customer must pay for resultant system upgrades

 introduces a first-mover problem that could stifle economic growth and slow grid expansion, both

        Oncor recommends eliminating the language from the rule that requires large load

not be required but for the interconnecting large load customer." Networked assets, including

those constructed as part of system upgrades, inherently benefit the entirety of the Texas grid, not

responsibility of that load through a CIAC payment. Radial lines and wider system upgrades on
